$comment: Every cut, label and camera move in this film lives in this file; src/ only reads it.
Frame numbers inside a scene are RELATIVE to that scene's first frame. `inFrame` is the
trim-in against the source clip, `durationInFrames` the length on the timeline. Those two
numbers ARE the cut. The camera is a keyframe list: scale and origin interpolate together
between entries, so a move is written as where the camera is at a moment, not as a verb.
Origins are fractions of the frame.
v5, ~90.5s: the v4 story told at walking pace. The note back on the 40-second cut was that
viewers got disoriented and phones could not read the text, so v5 changes three things at
once. The TAKE is new (footage/thread.mp4, 84s): performed at 1280x720 CSS under a 1.5
deviceScaleFactor, so the same 1920x1080 frame carries UI half again as large, typed at
30cps instead of 58 and held on every payoff. The CAMERA breathes on a fixed rhythm —
establish wide, push hard onto the one thing happening, HOLD long enough to read it at
phone scale, release wide before the next thing — with a dedicated wide breather after
Claude's answer. And the film gains one scene v4 deferred: Claude's reply ends with the
room-protocol footer and the drawer renders it as its own chip, 'answered - 3 rpm is Mars,
not the Moon - over to @codex' (drawer.js envRow/ENV_NEXT) — the one honest way the
shipped UI shows an agent handing the thread to the other agent. The summon stays with the
reader (bridge-system-prompt.md rule 6; server.mjs summons only on a person's message), so
the next scene is the reader ratifying the handoff.
Cue times and label positions are not guessed — capture/capture.mjs marks the instant AND
the frame-px box of every real action (footage/shots.json; boxes are measured in CSS px
and scaled through the shoot's deviceScaleFactor by rig.mjs), every `at`/`inFrame` below
is one of those marks, and a label names the mark it is placed against. Change a duration
and music/compose.mjs re-derives its arrangement from the same sums.
ON ORIGINS. src/Camera.tsx refuses to show the void: at scale s the origin is clamped to
1/(2s) from each edge, so the reachable range at 1.32 is 0.379..0.621 and at 1.50 it is
0.333..0.667. Every origin below is inside its own scale's range, so the file says what
the camera does. 'the drawer, right edge flush' is 1 - 1/(2s); the v5 drawer is 630 frame
px wide (420 CSS x 1.5), columns 1290..1920, so the green scene must reach 1.50 before a
left-flush window excludes it entirely.
ON LABELS. No label is at the top of the frame and none is centred over its action. A
label either hangs off a MEASURED box (`anchorMark` + `place`, projected through this
scene's camera at the current frame) or sits in the bottom-right corner — and v5 sets
them at 40px, because a 27px label at phone width was 5.6px of grey. Beats that read on
their own get none.

scenes.title: Google-Docs comments on any blog — with agents in the thread.
scenes.rationale: Say the thing, then show it. Four seconds now instead of v4's under-three: the sentence is the viewer's only map of the next ninety seconds, and the first note on the fast cut was that people never got oriented. Hard cut out — a dissolve would say the card and the product are one picture, and they are a claim and its evidence.

The post, held at its top long enough to actually read the title and the byline, then a reader's eased scroll down to the paragraph — 2.2s of scroll this time, not 1.5. Nothing in the product happens here and it is still the only part of the film that says WHERE this is happening: a real blog, its real typeface, the author's own logomark on the nav. The camera barely moves; the scroll is the motion.

The drag, slower than v4 (26 steps at 60ms — the whole proposition is that a sentence in a blog is a thing you can grab, so the grabbing is watchable now), then the pill. The camera pushes in ON the drag and holds through the pill click. The sage-green mark two sentences above is in the same shot on purpose: a resolved thread already existed here before the film started.

The drawer has arrived. First a beat WIDE — page and drawer in one frame, so a first-time viewer knows the new panel and the highlighted sentence are the same place — then the push onto the composer while the question is typed at reading speed (30cps; v4's 58 was the speed people called too fast). The question is the one this passage actually raises: the post states a diameter and two spin rates, and artificial gravity is one line of arithmetic away.

The working chip: claude's ring spinning under the question, a stop button beside it. It is the smallest thing in the film and it gets its own tight shot, two seconds now, because it is the only frame that says a real agent is being waited on rather than a canned answer being revealed.

The answer, streaming in and then held: w^2 r at r = 37.5 m, 3 rpm landing on 0.38 g, which is Mars and not the Moon. This is the frame that has to survive being paused AND being read on a phone, so the camera starts tight on the arriving words and eases back only far enough to hold the two bullets, then stays still for over three seconds of pure reading time.

The new scene, and the reason v5 exists beyond pacing: Claude's own reply ends with the room-protocol footer and the drawer draws it as a chip — status dot, 'answered', the one-line summary, 'over to @codex'. This is the shipped UI showing one agent handing the thread to the other (drawer.js envRow/ENV_NEXT), filmed as-is. What it is NOT is a summon: rule 6 of the bridge system prompt forbids a bot @-tagging its counterpart to summon it and server.mjs only summons on a person's message, so the film gives the chip its own tight shot and then hands the routing back to the reader, which is the only version of this that is true.

The zoom-out the v4 cut never took. Two seconds wide — the page, the yellow highlight, the open drawer, the cursor travelling to the composer — so a viewer who has been nose-against-the-glass for twenty seconds is re-anchored before the second half starts. The storyboard calls this the release half of the zoom rhythm; it is a shot of nothing happening, and it is load-bearing.

The reader ratifies the handoff Claude proposed: '@codex plot gravity vs radius at 2, 3 and 5 rpm?' typed into the same composer, under the same quote. No label — a second @-name typed after a chip that said 'over to @codex' is a sentence the viewer has already read.

The same chip, the other agent, the same length, the same framing height off the message it waits under. Repeating the shot exactly is the point: the second dial is what tells you the first one was a state and not a flourish.

Codex's reply, and the thing at the bottom of it: a python block, every line inside 43 characters so nothing clips, with a Run button under it that nobody has pressed. The drawer scrolls the cell to centre inside the shot, which is motion enough; the camera only leans.

The surprising feature, so it gets the tightest framing in the film, and the push happens BEFORE the click — a viewer has to know where to look while the cursor is still travelling or the Run button reads as an accident. Then a pull back timed to the figure painting. The label sits to the LEFT of the button, clear of the status line that prints underneath it: 'ran - 214 ms' is small type and it is half the payoff. The plot is real matplotlib output from the code on screen.

Full size, in the drawer's own lightbox, held for almost five seconds — because a thumbnail in a drawer is not a plot anybody reads, and because on a phone this is the one frame where the axes labels are genuinely legible. The picture settles the argument: at the crimson 37.5 m line the 3 rpm curve crosses Mars and the 5 rpm curve crosses Earth. No label; the axes are the label.

One click. The tick, the card leaving the list, and the count under it going 1 to 2. A small push rides the cursor to the tick so the eye arrives with it; after the click the camera holds almost still, because the motion is the list and a move would steal it. No label — a tick that empties a list explains itself.

The archive, open, with both filed cards in it — and the written paragraph landing over the 'summarizing...' placeholder while you watch. This is the scene people repeat, so it stays the longest thread scene in the film and now holds over three seconds AFTER the paragraph lands, which is what it costs to read four lines at phone scale. Both cards are visible on purpose: one was already there when the film started, so the shape of the archive is established rather than asserted. The label goes to the corner, because every position beside the paragraph is on top of the paragraph.

labels.text: Filing a thread writes the summary.

scenes.rationale: Back to the page, and the idea the whole beat sells: the mark stays. Both passages are sage green now — the one that was green before the camera rolled and the one that turned during it, two sentences apart in the same paragraph — so 'green means settled' is shown by a pair rather than explained by a caption. The v5 drawer is 630 frame px wide, so only a 1.50+ window flushed to the LEFT edge excludes it entirely; anything looser leaves an unreadable strip of it down the right edge, which is worse than either having it or not.

The note, in the vault. The BODY is frontends/plugin/export.mjs's own renderNote() output — the properties block, the title, the passage as a blockquote, 'Resolved by angadh' and the exchange under it — and the room around it is a recreation of Obsidian's dark reading view: the ribbon, the file tree with this note selected and the copied figure sitting in attachments/ under its real sha1 name, the tab strip, Inter at a readable line width. Shot in the same 1.5x geometry as the thread, so the note's 20px body type reaches the frame at 30px. The camera does not move at all — any scale above 1.0 would crop the ribbon and the tree, which are half of what the shot is for — so the motion is the note's own slow scroll.

A hard cut down the same document rather than a pan: two thousand pixels of note past a 1080 frame is a whoosh nobody can read, and the film's own rule is that cuts carry the pace. The foot is the point anyway — the code cell is in the vault with Obsidian's own syntax colours on it, the plot is in the vault as a copied attachment, and the attachment is visible in the sidebar as a file with a name.

scenes.title: botference Discuss
scenes.subtitle: botference.com
scenes.rationale: The braid entered late, where the three strands have already converged and 'the plan' has wiped out to the cursor — the site's own hero, filmed off its own markup rather than re-drawn, so it cannot drift from the real one. The type and the QR land together at frame 10 and hold: a code somebody is meant to scan off a playing video needs to be still, unfaded and large for long enough to acquire, which is over six seconds here against a 2.5-second floor. The url line is 38px now, for the same phone the QR is for.
